attestations.notes: Proof 1.1–4.1 read: nonempty first-order domain supplies one set, Separation with z != z gives an empty subset, and Extensionality proves uniqueness. No global choice is used.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: x != empty supplies a single B in x; Separation bounds the intersection by B, and the universal membership clause makes it independent of B. The empty-family intersection is excluded.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: the weak Power Set axiom provides a containing set; Separation removes extra members and Extensionality proves uniqueness, including x empty.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: all five identities follow from the union/intersection membership predicates; singleton and pair intersection families are nonempty even when a or b is empty. Binary union/intersection equalities are identified as definitions.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: a,b in A union B imply both singleton/pair components belong to its power set, hence the Kuratowski pair belongs to the double power set. Empty A or B leaves no given elements.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: both implications of unordered-pair equality are proved; the a=b branch handles singleton collapse and the distinct branch forces the other matching. The singleton consequence follows by b=a.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: unordered-pair equality applied to Kuratowski components gives two exhaustive matchings, both forcing a=c and b=d, including collapsed pairs; substitution proves the converse.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: both coordinates of each pair in R lie in union union R; Separation there gives precisely domain and range, including R empty. No selection of coordinate witnesses across R is needed.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: Separation inside one Infinity witness intersects all inductive classes via a first-order predicate; empty and successor closure hold, and mutual inclusion proves uniqueness.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: the induction subset is inductive, minimality of omega gives the reverse inclusion, and Separation converts definable properties to subsets. Both set and property forms are established.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: simultaneous induction proves transitivity and irreflexivity. Each possible self-membership of the successor forces n in n; no Foundation shortcut is required.

Proof 1.1–6.1 read: intersect all closed subsets of N x A, prove totality by Peano induction, then remove a hypothetical extra value at zero or successor to contradict minimality. Injectivity and nonzero successors justify closure of each deletion; uniqueness follows by equal-value induction. a in A excludes empty A.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: induction supplies P3; successor contains its predecessor and is nonzero; equality of distinct successors would imply mutual membership and violate transitivity/irreflexivity. All three Peano axioms follow.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: recursion with A=N, a=m, f=successor gives a unique total s_m; its value defines the total binary operation and both recursion equations. Uniqueness avoids any choice of s_m.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on c establishes addition associativity directly from right-zero and right-successor recursion, with a,b fixed arbitrarily.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on n proves 0+n=n using the right-successor recursion; n+0=n is the defining clause. Zero base is explicit.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on n proves the left-successor law; the successor step uses the right recursion twice, including its reverse substitution.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the zero base uses left identity, and the successor step combines right recursion with the proved left-successor law; induction gives commutativity.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on k cancels a common right summand; the successor step reduces equality by injectivity of successor. Zero summand is explicit.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the subset of zero and successors contains zero and is successor-closed independently of the hypothesis; induction exhausts N and n!=0 removes the zero branch.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: incompatibility of strict comparisons uses cancellation and nonzero successors; induction on n gives comparability with arbitrary m, splitting the positive difference into a successor. The n=0 and equal-value cases are explicit.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: additive witnesses prove reflexivity and transitivity; a zero sum forces each summand zero, and cancellation gives antisymmetry. Previously proved trichotomy supplies totality.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: both directions convert positive additive differences to successor differences; cancellation excludes equality in the reverse direction. The no-intermediate-element consequence uses the already established linear order.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: every relation pair lies in the product of its domain/range; both directions of the ambient product criterion follow from coordinate equality. All arguments remain vacuous for empty R.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: inverse and composite are separated inside the stated Cartesian products; restriction is separated inside R. Formulas use existential coordinates, not a family of choices, and cover empty relations.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: zero base follows from successor nonzeroness; successor injectivity reduces a fixed-point equation to the forbidden predecessor fixed point. Induction covers N.

Proof 1.1–6.1 read: induction first proves omega transitive; mixed order transitivity and discreteness establish m<successor(n) iff m<=n. Two independent inductions equate strict order and membership, then inclusion is equated with weak order using irreflexivity. Zero and successor clauses are explicit; no ordinal result is used.

Proof 1.1–7.1 read: a codomain transposition normalizes the hypothetical injection at the top point, then restriction misses that value and contradicts the induction hypothesis. Zero has no value for its singleton source. Restrictions prove the strict-size and N cases; another explicit transposition handles proper subsets. Bijection inverse plus trichotomy proves finite uniqueness; only one local witness is selected.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: under no least element, the initial-segment-avoidance set contains zero and is successor-closed. Discreteness plus successor injectivity justify m<successor(n) implies m<=n. Induction would make S empty, contradicting its hypothesis.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: fixed-m addition is a total self-map of N, so recursion with initial zero gives unique p_m and both multiplication clauses. The parameterized total operation needs no choice.
Proof 1.1–2.1 read: reassociation/commutation transports the additive witness in both directions, with cancellation for the reverse; cancellation also transports inequality, including k=0.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: right unit follows immediately from multiplication recursion and left additive identity. Simultaneous induction gives left zero and left unit, including n=0.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on c proves left distributivity; the complete second induction in 1.3 proves successor-left multiplication using additive reassociation and the successor recursion. Both zero bases are explicit.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: zero base uses left zero multiplication; recursion and the proved successor-left law identify the two successor products. Induction gives commutativity.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: zero base is explicit, and distributivity converts the successor expansion of (ab)c into a(bc+b). Induction gives associativity.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: positive m,n have successor presentations; multiplication plus addition recursion expresses mn as a successor, so it is nonzero. Contraposition gives the zero-divisor formulation.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: distributivity multiplies an additive order witness; with k!=0 a positive difference stays nonzero, and additive cancellation rules out equal products. k=0 is included only in weak monotonicity.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: adding the two representative-equivalence equations and regrouping proves addition descends; reversing the first equation proves negation descends. The quotient convention is a+bprime=b+aprime.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: both cross-sums factor through the common value a+bprime=b+aprime, proving independence of the first factor; symmetry of the pair product transfers this to the second. Sequential substitution proves full representative independence.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: representative independence licenses fixed-pair computations; each ring axiom is checked explicitly, including both coordinates of triple multiplication and distributivity. The inverse pair sums to the zero class.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: adding cross-sums proves invariance under each representative change in both directions; natural translation invariance gives transitivity and additive compatibility. Positive integer gaps k,m are nonzero naturals; expanding xy exposes the positive gap km. Reflexivity follows immediately from natural reflexivity, though not separately numbered.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: distributivity gives 0a=0a+0a, and additive identity followed by cancellation gives 0a=0. The cancellation uses commutativity of field addition.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: differences of translated elements are unchanged; differences of summed inequalities add in the positive cone. Both claimed strict inequalities follow, for arbitrary c in translation.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: distributivity and zero multiplication identify the opposite products as additive inverses; inverse uniqueness and double negation prove both sign identities. Zero inputs cause no exception.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: cone multiplication and negation identities prove the three product sign rules and forward order transport; trichotomy eliminates equality and the opposite comparison in each reverse direction. c=0 is expressly outside both transport claims.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: nonzero a has exactly one of the two strict signs; cone multiplication and (-a)^2=a^2 prove positivity in both cases. a=0 is excluded.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: field nontriviality supplies 1!=0, and the positive-square result applied to 1^2=1 gives the claim.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: a positive element has a nonzero inverse; a negative inverse would make 1 negative, contradicting positivity. Multiplication by the positive product of inverses reverses the comparison between positive a,b.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: additive identity/inverse uniqueness are explicit abelian-group calculations; the same arguments in F minus zero establish multiplicative uniqueness. Final step explicitly restricts multiplicative inversion to x!=0.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: all three nonzero sign patterns yield nonzero products in the ordered ring; distributivity reduces cancellation with z!=0 to (x-y)z=0. x-y may be zero and that is exactly the conclusion.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: cross-multiplication verifies product, sum, and negation under both representative changes using integer ring laws. Denominators are nonzero by hypothesis; their products remain nonzero by integer no-zero-divisors supplied through the rational-operation definition.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: all ring axioms are checked on rational representatives; distributivity compares the pair with its nonzero common scaling, and a nonzero numerator gives the inverse pair (b,a). Denominator closure uses integer no-zero-divisors; 1!=0 follows from the integer construction.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: positive-denominator representatives allow multiplication and cancellation of inequalities by positive integers. Cross-products prove representative independence, transitivity, additive compatibility, and positive-product closure. Reflexivity is immediate from integer reflexivity.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: evaluating e*f by each one-sided identity forces equality; this proves both consequences for a two-sided identity. Associativity is not used; hypotheses supply elements and thus exclude empty S.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: associativity equates h*(g*hprime) and (h*g)*hprime, yielding equality of opposing one-sided inverses. The three consequences retain the invertibility qualification when using only one inverse equation.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: positivity and adjacent strict increase follow from 1_F>0 and recursion. Complete inductions establish additive and multiplicative compatibility, and finite iteration proves strict monotonicity on positive naturals. Zero is introduced only as the recursive convention, not claimed positive.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: quotient equations prove injection and arithmetic/order preservation. A nonnegative integer pair has a natural additive gap k, hence equals (k,0); conversely all such classes are nonnegative, and injectivity gives uniqueness.
